title: BI-RADS Assessment Categories 3, 4, and 5 — Follow-Up and Biopsy
text:
Category 3 means a likelihood of malignancy of 2% or less. It is used only after a complete diagnostic work-up, never at screening. Typical examples are a solitary non-calcified circumscribed solid mass, a focal asymmetry with no correlate on ultrasound, or a solitary group of round calcifications.

Category 3 findings are managed by surveillance rather than biopsy: usually a follow-up mammogram at 6 months, then bilateral mammograms at about 12 and 24 months. After about 2 to 3 years of stability, the finding is reassessed as benign (category 2), or earlier if it resolves. A biopsy may still be chosen after shared decision-making with the patient, for a valid clinical reason, or when follow-up is impractical. If the finding grows or changes suspiciously, it is upgraded and biopsied.

title: BI-RADS Assessment Categories 3, 4, and 5 — Follow-Up and Biopsy
text: Radiologic–pathologic concordance means that the biopsy result satisfactorily explains what was seen on imaging. For example, a fibroadenoma explains a well-defined oval mass. The radiologist who performed the biopsy determines concordance, documents it and communicates it. A discordant result needs a repeat image-guided biopsy or surgical excision. Follow-up after a benign concordant biopsy is individualised.

title: BI-RADS Assessment Categories 3, 4, and 5 — Follow-Up and Biopsy
section: What Happens After an Abnormal Mammogram?
text:
1. Additional diagnostic mammographic views or a breast ultrasound may be recommended to characterise the finding further.
2. If a biopsy is recommended (category 4 or 5), an image-guided core needle biopsy is the usual first procedure.
3. The pathology result is compared with the imaging to check that they agree (concordance).
4. If cancer is confirmed, staging and treatment planning begin with the care team.
5. If the biopsy shows a benign result that agrees with the imaging, follow-up imaging is scheduled as the radiologist advises.

An AI risk estimate does not replace this clinical workflow. A risk estimate of any level does not bypass the need for clinical assessment, imaging interpretation by a radiologist and, where indicated, biopsy.

section: BI-RADS Mass Descriptors — Margin, Shape, and Density
text: BI-RADS is the American College of Radiology's lexicon for describing breast imaging findings. The inputs in this app use the terms of the 4th edition, which the UCI Mammographic Mass data were coded with. The 5th edition (2013) and the BI-RADS v2025 update renamed or removed some of them, as noted under each term. Percentages quoted below come from specific published series and vary between studies; they are context, not a risk estimate for an individual.

title: BI-RADS Mass Descriptors — Margin, Shape, and Density
text: Margin is the border of a mass on the mammogram. Circumscribed margins are reassuring, while indistinct (ill-defined) and spiculated margins are suspicious.

title: BI-RADS Mass Descriptors — Margin, Shape, and Density
text: A circumscribed margin is well defined: at least 75% of the border is sharply demarcated, with an abrupt transition between the mass and the surrounding tissue. Circumscribed masses are usually benign; examples include fibroadenomas and cysts. In a large study of non-palpable, non-calcified, circumscribed solid masses followed with mammography, 19 of 1,403 (1.4%) proved malignant. That figure applies to that specific group, not to every circumscribed mass.

title: Breast Imaging Glossary — Patient and Clinician Reference
text: A mammogram is an X-ray of the breast and the primary tool for breast cancer screening. Digital mammography records the X-rays electronically, so images can be enhanced and stored. Digital breast tomosynthesis (3D mammography) takes images from several angles and reconstructs thin slices through the breast. It improves cancer detection in many women with dense breasts, although a large US study found no gain at later screening rounds in extremely dense breasts.

title: Breast Imaging Glossary — Patient and Clinician Reference
text:
BI-RADS (Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System) is the American College of Radiology's standardised lexicon, report structure, assessment-category scheme and audit system for mammography, ultrasound, MRI and contrast-enhanced mammography. Its final assessment categories are:
- Category 0: Incomplete — additional imaging and/or comparison with prior images is needed
- Category 1: Negative — routine screening
- Category 2: Benign — routine screening
- Category 3: Probably benign — short-interval follow-up, usually at 6 months
- Category 4: Suspicious — tissue diagnosis (subdivided 4A, 4B, 4C)
- Category 5: Highly suggestive of malignancy — tissue diagnosis
- Category 6: Known biopsy-proven malignancy

title: Breast Imaging Glossary — Patient and Clinician Reference
text: A breast cyst is a fluid-filled sac. On ultrasound, a simple cyst is circumscribed, round or oval, free of internal echoes (anechoic) and thin-walled, often with posterior acoustic enhancement; it is benign. Complicated cysts are also usually benign and may be aspirated if they cause symptoms. Complex cystic and solid lesions should be biopsied.

title: Breast Imaging Glossary — Patient and Clinician Reference
text: Sensitivity is the share of people with the disease whom a test correctly flags: true positives divided by all people with the disease. Specificity is the share of people without the disease whom the test correctly clears: true negatives divided by all people without it. Screening programmes trade one against the other, and most women recalled after a screening mammogram do not have cancer.

title: Breast Imaging Modalities Compared
text: A mammogram is a low-dose X-ray of the compressed breast, taken in two views of each breast. Full-field digital mammography records the image electronically. Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT, "3D mammography") takes several low-dose exposures from different angles and reconstructs thin slices, which reduces the overlap of tissue that hides or mimics masses on a 2D image.

title: Breast Imaging Modalities Compared
text: In US screening data, mammography finds roughly 80–87% of the cancers present (sensitivity), with a specificity of about 89%. Sensitivity is lower in dense breasts, by 10–29 percentage points across all ages. About 10% of screened women are recalled for more tests, about 5 cancers are found per 1,000 screens, and only about 4–5% of recalled women turn out to have cancer. Over ten years of annual screening, about half of US women have at least one false-positive result, and 7–17% of these have a biopsy.

text: Mammography is the only screening test shown in randomised trials to reduce breast cancer mortality. It is widely available, standardised through BI-RADS, and detects microcalcifications, an early sign of ductal carcinoma in situ that other modalities often miss.

title: Breast Imaging Modalities Compared
text: It uses ionising radiation, although the dose is small: about 0.28 mSv for a screening digital mammogram and 0.34 mSv for tomosynthesis, equivalent to roughly one to one and a half months of natural background radiation. title: Breast Cancer Risk Factors and Epidemiology
text:
Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in women worldwide. GLOBOCAN 2020 estimated about 2.3 million new cases and 685,000 deaths in 2020, roughly one in four cancers diagnosed in women. In the United States, SEER estimates about 322,000 new cases of female breast cancer and 42,000 deaths in 2026, and about 13% of women will be diagnosed with breast cancer during their lifetime.

Survival depends strongly on the stage at diagnosis. In US SEER data (diagnoses 2016–2022), five-year relative survival was 91.9% overall: about 100% for localized disease (confined to the breast), 87.5% for regional disease (spread to nearby lymph nodes) and 33.8% for distant metastatic disease. Relative survival compares patients with similar women without breast cancer, so a figure near 100% means almost no excess deaths within five years.

title: Breast Cancer Risk Factors and Epidemiology
text:
**Age**: After female sex, age is the strongest risk factor. Most breast cancers are diagnosed after age 50.

**Sex**: Female sex is the main risk factor. Male breast cancer accounts for under 1% of cases.

**Inherited mutations**: Women with a BRCA1 mutation have a 55–72% risk of breast cancer by age 70–80, and BRCA2 carriers 45–69%, depending on the study. TP53 mutations (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) carry a near-certain lifetime risk of some cancer, with breast cancer in about half of female carriers by age 70. PALB2 mutations raise breast cancer risk roughly five-fold, and ATM or CHEK2 mutations roughly two-fold.

**Family history**: One first-degree relative (mother, sister or daughter) with breast cancer raises risk about 1.8-fold, and two first-degree relatives about 2.9-fold. A relative diagnosed at a young age raises risk more than one diagnosed late in life.

title: Breast Cancer Risk Factors and Epidemiology
text:
**Personal history**: After breast cancer in one breast, the risk of a new cancer in the other breast is about 0.4% per year. Atypical ductal hyperplasia raises risk about four- to five-fold, and lobular carcinoma in situ about seven- to twelve-fold, relative to women without these findings.

**Reproductive factors**: Early menarche (first period before 12), late menopause (after 55), never having given birth, and a first pregnancy late in life each raise risk modestly, mainly through longer lifetime exposure to oestrogen.

title: Breast Cancer Risk Factors and Epidemiology
text:
**Physical inactivity**: In pooled studies, the most physically active women had a 12–21% lower risk of breast cancer than the least active, for both premenopausal and postmenopausal women.

**Obesity after menopause**: Higher body mass index raises postmenopausal breast cancer risk by roughly 12% for every 5 kg/m², because fat tissue produces oestrogen through the enzyme aromatase.

**Alcohol**: Risk rises with the amount consumed, by about 7% for every 10 g of alcohol (roughly one standard drink) per day, and even light drinking raises risk slightly.

**Menopausal hormone therapy**: Combined oestrogen–progestogen therapy raises breast cancer risk from the first years of use (about 1.6-fold during years 1–4 of current use), and some excess risk persists for more than ten years after stopping.

title: Breast Cancer Risk Factors and Epidemiology
text:
The ACR BI-RADS density categories are: A, almost entirely fatty (about 10% of women); B, scattered areas of fibroglandular density (about 40%); C, heterogeneously dense (about 40%); and D, extremely dense (about 10%). Nearly half of women aged 40 and over who have mammograms have dense breasts (category C or D).

Density matters twice. Dense tissue and many cancers both appear white on a mammogram, so density lowers mammographic sensitivity (masking). Dense breasts are also an independent risk factor: compared with category B, breast cancer risk is roughly 1.4–1.6 times higher in category C and 1.6–1.8 times higher in category D.

title: Breast Cancer Risk Factors and Epidemiology
text: The average lifetime risk for a woman in the United States is about 13%. Guidelines use lifetime-risk thresholds to decide who should receive supplemental MRI screening: the American Cancer Society recommends annual MRI with mammography for women with a lifetime risk of about 20–25% or greater, recommends against MRI screening when lifetime risk is below 15%, and finds the evidence insufficient between 15% and 20%. NCCN uses a residual lifetime risk of 20% or greater, calculated with a model based on comprehensive family history, as the threshold for its increased-risk screening schedule.

title: Safety Disclaimer — BreastCare AI Scope, Limitations, and Patient Guidance
text: BreastCare AI is a research and educational prototype. It estimates the probability that a breast mass is malignant from four values: the patient's age and three BI-RADS descriptors of the mass (shape, margin and density). The estimate comes from a statistical model trained on the UCI Mammographic Mass dataset, a public collection of 961 masses (831 with complete descriptors) from one German radiology institute between 2003 and 2006. The model was chosen by a fixed rule from a logistic regression and two LightGBM candidates; the app shows which model is currently served.

title: Breast Cancer Treatment Pathways
text: Breast cancer treatment is multimodal and individualised. The pathway depends on the stage, the tumour's biology (hormone-receptor and HER2 status, grade, and sometimes a genomic test), and the patient's age, other illnesses and preferences. Decisions are made by a multidisciplinary team; this document describes the main building blocks, not a recommendation for any individual.

title: Breast Cancer Treatment Pathways
text:
**Breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy)**: Removes the tumour with a rim of normal tissue and is usually followed by radiation therapy. For appropriately selected early-stage cancers it gives the same survival as mastectomy.

**Mastectomy**: Removes the whole breast. It is chosen when the tumour is large relative to the breast, when there are several tumours in different parts of the breast, after previous breast radiation, or by patient preference. Variants include skin-sparing and nipple-sparing mastectomy with reconstruction.

**Sentinel lymph node biopsy**: Removes the first lymph node(s) draining the breast to check for spread. When the sentinel nodes are clear, a full axillary dissection is avoided, which lowers the risk of lymphoedema.

title: Breast Cancer Treatment Pathways
text:
**Whole-breast radiation**: Standard after breast-conserving surgery. In the pooled randomised trials, radiation roughly halved the ten-year risk of recurrence and reduced breast cancer deaths by about one-sixth. Hypofractionated schedules of three to four weeks are standard, and a one-week, five-fraction schedule was non-inferior in a large UK trial.

**Partial-breast irradiation**: Treats only the area around the tumour bed over a shorter course, for selected low-risk patients.

**Post-mastectomy radiation**: Recommended when four or more lymph nodes are involved, the tumour is larger than 5 cm, or the margins are positive, and considered when one to three nodes are involved. It reduces chest-wall recurrence and, in node-positive disease, breast cancer deaths.

title: Breast Cancer Treatment Pathways
text:
**Chemotherapy**: Given before surgery (neoadjuvant) or after it (adjuvant). Common regimens are AC-T (doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel) and TC (docetaxel and cyclophosphamide). Neoadjuvant chemotherapy can shrink a tumour enough to allow breast conservation, and is standard for stage II–III triple-negative and HER2-positive cancers.

**Endocrine (hormonal) therapy**: For hormone receptor-positive cancers, which make up roughly 70–80% of breast cancers. Tamoxifen can be used before or after the menopause; aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) are used after the menopause, or before it together with ovarian suppression. Treatment lasts at least five years and up to ten for higher-risk disease.

title: Breast Cancer Treatment Pathways
text:
**Targeted therapy**: HER2-positive cancers (about 15–20%) are treated with trastuzumab, often with pertuzumab, and with the antibody–drug conjugates T-DM1 and trastuzumab deruxtecan. CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) are standard with endocrine therapy for advanced hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative disease, and abemaciclib and ribociclib are also used for high-risk early disease. PARP inhibitors (olaparib, talazoparib) are used for HER2-negative cancers in carriers of a germline BRCA mutation, including olaparib after surgery for high-risk early cancers.

**Immunotherapy**: Pembrolizumab with chemotherapy is used for early-stage triple-negative breast cancer (before and after surgery, regardless of PD-L1 status) and for PD-L1-positive metastatic triple-negative disease.

title: Breast Cancer Treatment Pathways
text:
**Stage 0 (ductal carcinoma in situ)**: Breast-conserving surgery with radiation, or mastectomy. Endocrine therapy may be offered for oestrogen receptor-positive DCIS to lower the risk of a new cancer. Chemotherapy is not used.

**Stage I**: Breast-conserving surgery with radiation (preferred) or mastectomy, with sentinel node biopsy. Systemic therapy depends on receptor status and, for hormone receptor-positive HER2-negative cancers, often on a genomic test.

**Stage II**: Surgery is chosen according to tumour and breast size, with axillary staging. Neoadjuvant therapy is often used, both to allow breast conservation and, in triple-negative and HER2-positive disease, to tailor treatment after surgery to the response.

**Stage III (locally advanced)**: Neoadjuvant systemic therapy to shrink the tumour, then surgery and radiation, with further systemic treatment as indicated.

title: Breast Cancer Treatment Pathways
text:
**Oncotype DX**: A 21-gene recurrence score for hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer. In the TAILORx trial, women with scores of 0–10 did well with endocrine therapy alone, and for scores of 11–25 endocrine therapy alone was not inferior to adding chemotherapy overall, although women aged 50 or younger with scores of 16–25 gained some benefit from chemotherapy. Scores of 26 or above indicate a likely chemotherapy benefit.

**MammaPrint**: A 70-gene signature classifying tumours as low or high genomic risk. In the MINDACT trial, women at high clinical risk but low genomic risk had good outcomes without chemotherapy.

title: WHO Breast Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis
text: The WHO position paper on mammography screening (2014) recommends organised, population-based mammography screening only in well-resourced settings where the health system can guarantee quality assurance, follow-up of abnormal results and treatment. It recommends biennial screening of women aged 50–69 in such settings. Screening women aged 40–49 or 70–75 is suggested only within rigorous research or in programmes that can show their net benefit. Screening without the capacity to diagnose and treat the cancers found causes harm, through false positives, overdiagnosis and overtreatment, without the benefit.

title: WHO Breast Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis
text:
**Well-resourced settings**: Organised programmes offering biennial mammography to women aged 50–69, with quality assurance, defined follow-up pathways and monitoring of performance.

**Limited-resource settings with relatively strong health systems**: Mammography screening is not recommended as the first priority. The WHO suggests investing first in early diagnosis of symptomatic disease and in treatment capacity, and considering screening only once those are in place.

**Limited-resource settings with weak health systems**: Focus on breast cancer awareness and timely diagnosis and treatment of symptomatic women. Clinical breast examination as a screening method should be offered only within research, because its effect on mortality has not been established.

**Limited-resource settings with relatively strong health systems**: Mammography screening is not recommended as the first priority. The WHO suggests investing first in early diagnosis of symptomatic disease and in treatment capacity, and considering screening only once those are in place.

**Limited-resource settings with weak health systems**: Focus on breast cancer awareness and timely diagnosis and treatment of symptomatic women. Clinical breast examination as a screening method should be offered only within research, because its effect on mortality has not been established.

title: WHO Breast Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis
text: The WHO Global Breast Cancer Initiative (2021) aims to reduce breast cancer mortality by 2.5% per year, averting 2.5 million deaths between 2020 and 2040. It sets three targets: at least 60% of invasive breast cancers diagnosed at stage I or II (health promotion for early detection); diagnostic evaluation completed within 60 days of first presentation (timely diagnosis); and at least 80% of patients completing multimodality treatment (comprehensive management).

title: WHO Breast Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis
text: In the randomised trials, inviting women aged 50–69 to mammographic screening reduced breast cancer mortality by about 20%; observational studies of women who actually attend suggest a larger reduction, around 40%. For women aged 40–49 the reduction in the trials was smaller, around 15%, with more false positives per cancer found. Screening has not been shown to reduce deaths from all causes.

title: WHO Breast Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis
text: Overdiagnosis is the detection of a cancer that would never have caused symptoms in the woman's lifetime. Estimates vary widely with the method used, from under 10% to more than 50% of screen-detected cancers. The UK Independent Review (2012) estimated that about 19% of cancers diagnosed by screening are overdiagnosed, equivalent to roughly 11% of all cancers diagnosed in invited women. Low-grade ductal carcinoma in situ accounts for a large share.

title: WHO Breast Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis
text: European guidelines set programme standards: double reading of mammograms by two readers; a recall rate below 7% at the first (prevalent) screen and below 5% at later (incident) screens; a cancer detection rate of at least three times the background incidence at the first screen and 1.5 times at later screens; and interval cancers below 30% of background incidence in the first year after screening and below 50% in the second. In the United States, the American College of Radiology's minimum standards for an individual radiologist include a sensitivity of at least 75% and a cancer detection rate of at least 2.5 per 1,000 examinations.

title: WHO Breast Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis
text: The WHO Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis (2017) describes three steps: awareness of symptoms and access to care; clinical evaluation, diagnosis and staging; and access to treatment. It advises that the interval from first presentation to the start of treatment should be as short as possible, with treatment starting within about a month of diagnosis and no more than about 90 days passing from first symptoms to treatment.
